hints: Focus on what type of structure and bonding sodium and potassium both have as Group 1 metals.
Remember both form +1 cations in a sea of delocalised electrons, but $Na^+$ is smaller than $K^+$ so its charge density is higher.
Think about which description correctly names metallic bonding and explains why more energy is needed to melt sodium.
walkthrough:
**Identify the bonding type**

Both sodium and potassium are metals, so they both have giant metallic lattices. There are no molecules, no anions, and no shared pairs here.

Model: $M^+ \text{ cations in a sea of delocalised } e^-$

**Recall what controls melting point**

Melting breaks down the attraction between the positive cations and the delocalised electrons. Stronger metallic bonding means more heat energy is needed, so a higher melting point.

**Compare sodium and potassium**

Both donate one electron to the sea, so charge is the same (+1). The difference is size. $Na^+$ is smaller than $K^+$ because potassium has an extra electron shell.

Charge density: $$\text{charge density of } Na^+ > \text{charge density of } K^+$$

**Link size to strength**

The smaller $Na^+$ attracts the delocalised electrons more strongly. That stronger cation to electron attraction gives sodium stronger metallic bonding and a higher melting point than potassium.

options.A: Correct. This is the exact definition of metallic bonding. The smaller $Na^+$ ion has a higher charge density than $K^+$, so it holds the delocalised electrons more tightly, giving stronger bonding and a higher melting point.
options.B: Incorrect. Cations and anions attract in ionic bonding, not in pure metals. Sodium and potassium metals contain only cations and delocalised electrons, there are no anions present.
options.C: Incorrect. Saying attraction between atoms is too vague and describes simple covalent or van der Waals forces. It does not name the metallic bonding model of cations plus delocalised electrons that examiners want.
options.D: Incorrect. Nuclei and shared electron pairs describe covalent bonding. Sodium and potassium do not share pairs between two nuclei, they donate electrons to a delocalised sea.
